Let's dive into Chapter 3: Overcoming Barriers to Living with Intention.
Even when you really get how powerful intention is—and you know its seven qualities—life still has a way of throwing up some roadblocks. These obstacles aren’t always out in the open. More often, they sneak in as old habits, limiting beliefs, or that persistent little voice of the ego.
The ego is especially sneaky, isn’t it? It’ll whisper that your value depends on what you accomplish, what you own, or whether other people approve of you. It convinces you that it’s all about separation—me against them, winning or losing. And that kind of thinking? It just breeds scarcity and competition, making it really tough to trust in the abundance and connection that living with intention brings.
Maybe you know someone—maybe it’s even you—who spent years chasing promotions, believing that the next title would finally bring happiness. But after each achievement, that satisfaction just faded away, replaced by anxiety about the next goal. It often takes a pause, a moment to ask, “Why am I doing this?” to realize how much of that drive is coming straight from the ego.
Limiting beliefs are another big hurdle. These are those quiet, almost invisible assumptions we pick up from family, culture, or past experiences. Things like, “I’m not creative,” or “I don’t deserve success,” or even, “Things never work out for me.” These thoughts work in the background, shaping your choices and expectations—usually without you even noticing.
Picture someone who grew up always hearing that money was tight, and that only a lucky few ever get ahead. Fast forward, and as an adult, they keep sabotaging themselves, convinced that abundance is just out of reach. But when they start to question those old beliefs—and swap them out for new ones—their life starts to shift, too.
And then, there’s fear. Fear of failing, fear of what others might say, fear of the unknown—it can all add up and leave you feeling stuck. Think about a young artist who keeps their work hidden for years, terrified of criticism. But when they finally step out and share their art, they find not just acceptance, but encouragement and support.
Here’s some good news: these barriers don’t have to last forever. You can notice them, and you can let them go—often with some simple practices. Visualization, for example, lets you imagine new possibilities and see yourself succeeding. Affirmations—those positive statements you repeat—can start to rewire old thought patterns. And meditation? It creates space for new insights, quiets the ego, and helps you hear the voice of intention more clearly.
The key isn’t to wipe out all doubt or become completely fearless. It’s about seeing when these barriers pop up and choosing to respond in a new way. Over time, the ego’s grip gets weaker, those limiting beliefs lose their power, and fear gives way to curiosity and trust.
Most people find out that the real transformation isn’t about changing the world outside, but changing how they see themselves—and their place in it. Once that inner landscape shifts, you’ll start to notice the outer world reflecting those changes right back at you.
